Electric basses, each with its real control layout. Pick any two, set one, and translate the setting to the other. Click a heading to fold or open it. The guitars are on [Electric Guitars Compared](guitar-compare.qmd); the model is the same.

::: {.ik-do}
**What you'll do**

1. Learn what changes when the pickup model hears a bass string instead of a guitar string.
2. Hear the split-coil P pickup, the Jazz Bass blend, and an active EQ.
3. Translate a sound from one bass to another and read what is lost.
:::

## What is different on a bass

- **A longer, heavier string.** Fender chose a 34-inch scale for the Precision (Wikipedia, "Fender Precision Bass"); the Rickenbacker's is 33.5 in (Wikipedia, "Rickenbacker 4001"). The open E is 41 Hz, so the harmonics a pickup hears are lower and closer together.
- **The comb filter is the same idea** as on a guitar (Tillman, 2002): a harmonic with a still point over the pickup is not heard. Near the bridge: more high harmonics, a brighter sound.
- **The split coil (Precision, from 1957).** Two coils, each under two strings, wired out of phase with reversed magnets, so hum cancels (Wikipedia, "Fender Precision Bass"). On this page the E and A strings hear one half and the D and G strings the other.
- **The blend (Jazz Bass).** No switch: two volume knobs. The two single coils are reverse wound and reverse polarity, so hum cancels with both full up (Wikipedia, "Fender Jazz Bass"). Both together add their combs: "the classic scooped, 'growling' sound" (Wikipedia).
- **60s vs 70s spacing.** The Jazz Bass's pickups were 3.6 in apart until late 1970; then the bridge pickup moved 0.4 in nearer the bridge (Wikipedia). Both are here: **Jazz 1960s** and **Jazz 1970s**.
- **Active EQ (StingRay).** A preamp inside the bass, on a 9-volt battery (Wikipedia, "Music Man StingRay"), can boost as well as cut, and it stops the cable dulling the pickup. 2-band at first, a mid band added later (Wikipedia).

## The basses side by side

Choose a bass for each side. Drag a knob (arrow keys work too), click a switch and press a ▶ button. The picture shows the harmonics of the open A string (55 Hz) at the jack (bars) and the circuit alone (line). **Amp** sends the sound through the site's amp model (the one on [Gear 3](gear-amps.qmd)); **Strings: Band samples** plays the band's bass samples through the circuit only. The ☀ / ☾ button switches every panel between a white and a black background.

## Translating between basses

**Translate** finds the setting on the other bass that sounds most like this one: it tries every switch position, tone setting, Jazz volume blend and (on the StingRays) EQ setting, and compares the share of sound in third-octave bands for three open strings. The report says:

- **exact**: the same kind of pickups in the same places, and almost the same sound;
- **approx**: the closest setting, with notes on what differs (for example the P's split coil on a Jazz Bass, or an active boost on a passive bass);
- **lost**: nothing comes close.

Try a StingRay with the treble boosted to the P-Bass, or the 3-band's mid boost to the 2-band.

## What is this site's own

- Every pickup's inductance, resistance and capacitance, the pot and capacitor values, the string's stiffness and decay, and every pickup distance from the bridge are this site's estimates (unverified; `apps/shared/lessons/bass-pickups.js`). Only the Jazz Bass's 3.6 / 4 in pickup spacing is from a source.
- Which half of the P pickup is nearer the bridge, the Jazz Bass's volume wiring (a volume at 0 solos the other pickup), and every number of the StingRay preamp (gain, EQ frequencies, ±15 dB, 5 = flat, knob order) are this site's (unverified).
- The drawings are after photos, not measured drawings; no makers' logos. Nobody has compared the sound with real basses.

## Works Cited

<!-- works-cited: written by scripts/works-cited.py -->
::: {.works-cited}
"Fender Jazz Bass." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fender_Jazz_Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fender_Jazz_Bass). 1960 (Deluxe Model); two single coils, two poles a string, RWRP, hum cancels with both full; stacked knobs, then from late 1961 two volumes + master tone; pickups 3.6 in apart until late 1970, then 4 in (Fender: 1972); scooped growl (Marcus Miller); Jaco's 1962 Jazz.

"Fender Precision Bass." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fender_Precision_Bass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fender_Precision_Bass). On sale October 1951; 34 in scale; split-coil pickup from 1957, coils wired out of phase with reversed magnets (hum-cancelling); Jamerson's 1962 Precision on Motown hits; signature models (Sting, Harris, Waters).

"Music Man StingRay." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Man_StingRay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_Man_StingRay). 1976; Leo Fender with Tom Walker (active preamp, 9 V); one large humbucker nearer the bridge, coils in parallel; 2-band EQ then a mid added; Deacon on Another One Bites the Dust, Edwards on Le Freak, Louis Johnson.

"Rickenbacker 4001." *Wikipedia*, Wikimedia Foundation, [en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rickenbacker_4001](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rickenbacker_4001). 4001 November 1961, 4003 1980 (truss rod for roundwounds); 33.5 in; toaster neck + horseshoe bridge pickups, later Hi-Gain; extra volume and tone, three-position switch; Ric-O-Sound 1968; Squire's bright twangy tone, Lemmy, Geddy Lee.

Tillman, J. Donald. "Response Effects of Guitar Pickup Position and Width." 2000, updated 17 Oct. 2002. [www.till.com/articles/PickupResponse/index.html](https://www.till.com/articles/PickupResponse/index.html). Pickup point response sin(pi x F / (L F0)) = a comb filter; aperture term; Strat neck / middle / bridge 6.375 / 3.875 / 1.625 in, 1 in aperture; humbucker about 2.5 in; out-of-phase cancellation.
:::
